summary: Vinorelbine is a semisynthetic vinca alkaloid given by short IV injection for advanced/metastatic non-small cell lung cancer, alone or combined with cisplatin. It carries a boxed warning for severe myelosuppression. It is a vesicant requiring careful IV administration to avoid extravasation, and the dose must be reduced for low neutrophil counts or elevated bilirubin.
indications: First-line treatment of locally advanced or metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) in combination with cisplatin
First-line treatment of metastatic NSCLC as a single agent

dosage.n: Cisplatin given Day 1 only of each cycle
Cisplatin Days 1 and 29, then every 6 weeks
Based on neutrophil count on day of treatment

admin: Administer only by intravenous route; intrathecal administration is fatal
Inject or infuse over 6 to 10 minutes
Vesicant - ensure correct needle/catheter placement; flush vein with fluid before and after
If extravasation occurs, stop immediately and manage per institutional protocol
Verify neutrophil count is adequate before each dose
moa: Vinca alkaloid that binds tubulin and interferes with microtubule assembly, inhibiting mitosis at metaphase; this antimitotic action produces its antitumor effect, with relative selectivity for mitotic over axonal microtubules.
preg: Can cause fetal harm based on mechanism and animal data; avoid in pregnancy. Females of reproductive potential should use effective contraception during and after therapy.
lact: Unknown if excreted in human milk; advise not to breastfeed during treatment and for a period after the final dose.
renal: No specific dose adjustment recommended; eliminated mainly via hepatobiliary route.
hepatic: Reduce dose with elevated serum total bilirubin (50% for 2.1-3 mg/dL; 25% for >3 mg/dL).

major: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., ketoconazole, ritonavir) - increased vinorelbine exposure and toxicity
Other myelosuppressive agents and radiation - additive bone marrow suppression
moderate: Mitomycin - reports of acute pulmonary reactions/bronchospasm
minor: Drugs causing peripheral neuropathy - additive neurotoxicity
interactions.diagnostics: Obtain CBC with neutrophil count before each dose; check bilirubin before dosing.

monitoring: Complete blood count with neutrophil count before each dose
Serum total bilirubin and liver enzymes
counsel: This chemotherapy is given by injection into a vein, usually weekly
Report fever, chills, or signs of infection immediately - your white cells may be low
Report constipation, severe abdominal pain, or numbness/tingling
Use effective contraception; do not breastfeed
Report any pain, swelling, or burning at the injection site during infusion
pk: Refrigerate 2-8 C; protect from light; do not freeze
pearls: Boxed warning: severe myelosuppression can cause serious infection, septic shock, and death
Vesicant - extravasation causes severe local tissue injury
Never give intrathecally - it is uniformly fatal
Granulocytopenia is dose-limiting and usually the reason to hold or reduce the dose
Reduce dose for hyperbilirubinemia, not for renal impairment
missed: Administered in a clinical setting on a set schedule; doses are timed to neutrophil recovery. A missed/held dose is rescheduled by the oncology team based on counts. Patients do not self-administer.
overdose: No specific antidote. Overdose may produce severe myelosuppression, ileus, and neurotoxicity. Provide supportive care including blood product/growth-factor support, infection prophylaxis/treatment, and management of ileus. Monitor closely.
